items.title: UK Corporate Governance Code 2024
items.locator: Section 4, Provision 29 (PDF page 14); Introduction, 'Application' and 'Reporting on the Code'
items.quote: a declaration of effectiveness of the material controls as at the balance sheet date
items.why: The source of the declaration. Applies to companies listed in the commercial companies category or the closed-ended investment funds category, on a comply-or-explain basis. Provision 29 takes effect a year after the rest of the 2024 Code. The Code does not mention AI.

items.title: Corporate Governance Code Guidance: Material controls
items.locator: Section 4, paragraphs 270 to 275; page last updated 3 June 2026
items.quote: information and technology risks including cybersecurity, data protection and new technologies (e.g. artificial intelligence)
items.why: Source of the quotation. The list is of controls that 'could include, but are not limited to'; the board decides which are material. Paragraph 274 says there is no requirement or expectation of external advice or assurance on the effectiveness of material controls. Guidance, not part of the Code.

items.title: Corporate Governance Code Guidance: Declaration on the effectiveness of the material controls
items.locator: Section 4, paragraphs 296 to 300
items.quote: The board can only provide a reasonable conclusion regarding the effectiveness of the controls, based on the work carried out and evidence obtained.
items.why: What 'honestly' means in practice: the declaration rests on work done and evidence. Paragraph 297 covers disclosing a control that is not operating effectively; paragraph 298 allows a board that cannot determine effectiveness to explain this under comply or explain.

items.title: Annual Review of Corporate Governance Reporting 2025
items.locator: Section 4, 'Reporting on the outcome of the review of effectiveness' (page 39), 'Provision 29' (pages 40 to 41) and 'Artificial Intelligence' (pages 44 to 45); sample described on page 5
items.quote: 40 companies did not report on the outcome.
items.why: Source of the figure, from a sample of 100 randomly selected companies reporting under the 2018 Code. Also found that 86% of companies mentioned AI, that three disclosed it as a principal risk, and that more than half mentioned the new provision. A sample of listed companies, before the declaration applied.

items.title: Cyber Governance Code of Practice
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Section E: Assurance and oversight, Actions 1 to 5; Glossary, 'Gain assurance'
items.quote: Require formal reporting on at least a quarterly basis, set suitable metrics to track, and agree tolerances for each.
items.why: The standard for boards outside the listed-company Code. Defines 'gain assurance' as obtaining confidence that controls are effective, often through audits, reviews or third-party validation, and asks that cyber considerations be consistent with internal and external audit. Voluntary.

items.title: Cyber Security Toolkit for Boards: Implementing effective cyber security measures
items.locator: Principle E, sections on testing the effectiveness of controls and on metrics; version 3.0, reviewed 8 April 2025
items.quote: testing the effectiveness of your security controls is important
items.why: Practical guidance behind the governance code: review measures against a framework, rehearse responses, and give the board metrics such as time to detect and recover. Says measures should be traceable to the risks they mitigate. Does not address AI controls specifically.

items.title: Cyber security breaches survey 2025/2026
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology and Home Office
items.locator: Section 2.2, 'Board responsibilities', Figures 2.6 to 2.8
items.quote: More than two-thirds of large businesses (68%) had a board member responsible for cyber security compared with 31% of businesses overall.
items.why: How far board ownership of security has spread. The survey notes that not all businesses have a formal board, which may lower the overall figure. It measures a named responsibility, not the quality of the evidence boards receive.

items.title: FCA Handbook, SYSC 15A: Operational resilience
items.locator: SYSC 15A.6.1R and 15A.7.1R (each dated 31/03/2022)
items.quote: A firm must ensure that its governing body approves and regularly reviews the written records required under
items.why: A binding parallel for regulated financial firms: the governing body must approve and regularly review the firm's written self-assessment of its operational resilience. A sector rule, separate from the listed-company declaration.

items.title: FCA, Bank of England and Treasury joint statement on frontier AI models and cyber resilience
items.locator: Section 'Governance and strategy'; footnote on status
items.quote: Firms should ensure their boards and senior management have sufficient understanding of frontier AI risks.
items.why: The most recent UK statement tying AI to board oversight of security. It is about AI used by attackers, not the firm's own AI systems, and says it is not intended to introduce new expectations.

items.title: Provision 29 Mythbuster: Preparing to report
items.locator: Questions 'How many material controls should we have?', 'Will boards have to seek external assurance over controls?' and 'How should the declaration be worded?'
items.quote: The Code does not state that the testing of the material controls should be supported by external assurance
items.why: The regulator's latest answers on the declaration: no list of controls or testing need be published, most companies report identifying between 30 and 50 material controls, no wording will be supplied, and external assurance is the board's choice. The PDF carries no date; the FRC's web version of it is dated 29 January 2026. Informal guidance, not part of the Code; it does not mention AI.

items.title: Mythbuster: the auditor's responsibilities in respect of the Provision 29 statement required by the UK Corporate Governance Code 2024
items.locator: Questions on whether the audit opinion covers the statement and whether the auditor tests the material controls
items.quote: the auditor is not required to test the design, implementation and operating effectiveness of the material controls identified by the Board
items.why: Settles who stands behind the declaration: the audit opinion does not cover it and the auditor only reads it for inconsistency with what the audit found. Any independent assurance on AI controls therefore has to be commissioned by the board. Informal guidance for stakeholders; auditing standards were not changed.

items.title: FCA Handbook, UK Listing Rules, UKLR 6.6: Annual financial report
items.quote: a statement as to whether the listed company has
items.why: The binding rule that gives the Code its force: a UK-incorporated listed company must state in its annual report whether it complied with all relevant provisions of the UK Corporate Governance Code and, if not, which and why. So a board that cannot make the declaration must say so publicly. Applies to listed companies only.

items.title: FCA Handbook, Disclosure Guidance and Transparency Rules, DTR 7.2: Corporate governance statements
items.quote: internal control and risk management systems in relation to the financial reporting process
items.why: A mandatory disclosure that sits beside the declaration: the corporate governance statement must describe the main features of internal control and risk management over financial reporting. Narrower than the declaration (financial reporting only, a description and not a conclusion on effectiveness). Issuers within DTR 7.2 only.

items.title: Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, section 404: Management assessment of internal controls
items.publisher: United States Congress (U.S. Government Publishing Office)
items.locator: Section 404(a) and (b); Public Law 107-204, 116 Stat. 789
items.quote: each registered public accounting firm that prepares or issues the audit report for the issuer shall attest to, and report on, the assessment
items.why: International comparator and the model the UK chose not to follow: US law requires management's assessment of internal control over financial reporting and the auditor's attestation of it. The UK declaration is wider (operational and compliance controls too) but unaudited. The Act as passed in 2002, read from the official print; later amendments are not shown there and were not checked.

items.title: Prudential Standard CPS 234 Information Security
items.locator: Sections 'Roles and responsibilities' and 'Testing control effectiveness'
items.quote: must escalate and report to the Board or senior management any testing results that identify information security control deficiencies
items.why: International comparator. A binding standard that makes the board ultimately responsible for information security and requires control testing by functionally independent specialists, with failures escalated. Shows what evidence-fed board assurance looks like when written as a rule. Australian regulated financial entities only; not AI-specific.

items.title: Final Notice: TSB Bank plc
items.locator: Paragraph 2.36(c); penalty at paragraph 1.1
items.quote: some assurances were limited or qualified in ways which do not appear to have been drawn to the TSB Board’s attention or challenged by them
items.why: Enforcement decision on board assurance over technology: the board received assurances about a new IT platform that were qualified in ways it was not told about and did not challenge. The FCA's penalty was £29.75 million. A 2018 IT migration at a bank, not an AI system, and decided under financial services rules, not the Code.

items.title: Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry: Final Report, Volume 1
items.publisher: Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry (Sir Wyn Williams)
items.locator: Chapter 1, Introduction, paragraphs 1.3 and 1.4; HC 1119
items.quote: the Post Office maintained the fiction that its data was always accurate
items.why: Statutory inquiry finding on what happens when an organisation asserts that a system works without evidence: senior staff knew or should have known it could produce false data, and people were prosecuted on its output. Volume 1 covers human impact and redress; findings on governance were left to a later volume. Not an AI system.

items.title: Trusted third-party AI assurance roadmap
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Section 'Challenges for a trusted third-party assurance market', under 'Quality'
items.quote: the quality of the goods and services provided is currently unclear
items.why: A caution on 'independently assured': the government's own assessment is that the quality of third-party AI assurance on the UK market is unclear, and that none of the existing certifications of assurance skills is issued by a UKAS-accredited organisation. A policy paper setting out plans, not a standard.

items.title: Auditing large language models: a three-layered approach
items.locator: Abstract
items.quote: existing auditing procedures fail to address the governance challenges posed by LLMs
items.why: Research from UK-based authors on what independent assurance of AI would have to cover: the supplier's governance, the model, and the application built on it. The abstract page links the published version in the journal AI and Ethics (2023); only the arXiv abstract was read. A proposal, not a tested method, and the authors discuss its limits.

items.title: Closing the AI Accountability Gap: Defining an End-to-End Framework for Internal Algorithmic Auditing
items.publisher: arXiv (Raji, Smart, White, Mitchell, Gebru, Hutchinson, Smith-Loud, Theron and Barnes)
items.locator: Abstract
items.quote: it remains challenging for practitioners to identify the harmful repercussions of their own systems prior to deployment
items.why: Research on producing the evidence a declaration needs: an internal audit process in which each stage yields documents that together form an audit report. Presented at the ACM fairness conference in 2020; a proposed framework, and the abstract reports no independent validation.
